reason: In Russia, even numbers of flowers are for funerals. A dozen roses as a gift reads as mourning.
suggested_fix: Use an odd number, e.g. "Удивите её букетом из 11 алых роз", or drop the count.

reason: Yellow flowers in Russia are widely read as a sign of separation or infidelity. They're a poor romantic gift.
suggested_fix: Change the color, e.g. "букетом нежных весенних цветов" or pink/white flowers.

reason: You go, girl! is American sassy slang with no natural Russian equivalent. Literal rendering sounds odd or patronizing.
suggested_fix: Use direct encouragement, e.g. "Вы справитесь! Достигайте своих целей."

reason: Piece of cake doesn't work literally in Russian and would read as being about dessert.
suggested_fix: Use "проще простого" or "пользоваться легко".

reason: Lettuce/Let us wordplay is untranslatable. The joke disappears in Russian.
suggested_fix: Drop the pun and lead with the offer, e.g. "Время салатов! Скидка 20% на все салаты."

reason: Whistling indoors is believed in Russia to drive money away. An office whistling image hits that directly. The Disney song reference is also weak.
suggested_fix: Drop the whistling, e.g. "Работайте под хорошую музыку: новый офисный плейлист уже здесь."

reason: The Super Bowl is not a meaningful cultural event in Russia, so the comparison doesn't land.
suggested_fix: Use a neutral superlative, e.g. "Распродажа года!"

reason: Fitta is vulgar slang for female genitalia in Swedish and Norwegian.
suggested_fix: Use a different name in Nordic markets. Honda sold the Fit there as "Jazz".

reason: Miss the boat doesn't carry over literally in Russian.
suggested_fix: Use "Не упустите шанс: распродажа заканчивается в пятницу."

reason: Literal rendering famously came out as "eat your fingers off" in Chinese. The idiom doesn't survive translation.
suggested_fix: Use an established equivalent, e.g. "吮指回味，自在滋味" or a simple "美味可口".

reason: Baseball idiom; baseball is niche in Russia, so the metaphor won't land when rendered literally.
suggested_fix: Drop the sports image and use a neutral success phrase, e.g. "Добейтесь большего с нашим новым планировщиком."

reason: Spring break is a US college tradition with no Russian counterpart. Russian spring school holidays are short and not tied to beach trips.
suggested_fix: Reframe around a local occasion, e.g. May holidays: "Майские праздники скоро! Бронируйте отдых на море."

reason: Literal Spanish renderings of "turn it loose" (e.g. "suéltalo") can read as "get diarrhea", a known slogan failure.
suggested_fix: Use a different energetic line, e.g. "Déjate llevar" or "Libera tu energía".

reason: Russia celebrates Mother's Day on the last Sunday of November, not in May. A May 10 date would confuse readers.
suggested_fix: Use the Russian date, or retarget the May campaign to March 8 (International Women's Day).

reason: Assume nothing is terse and easy to mistranslate as "do nothing". This is a known slogan failure.
suggested_fix: Brief translators on the intended meaning ("don't take anything for granted") and adapt per market, not literally.

reason: Embarrass is easily rendered as "embarazar", which means "to get pregnant" in Spanish.
suggested_fix: Use "avergonzar" or rephrase, e.g. "No se derramará en tu bolsillo ni te hará pasar vergüenza."

reason: Peanut butter and jelly sandwiches are not a familiar Russian lunch staple. The reference falls flat.
suggested_fix: Use a familiar food, e.g. "Возьмите бутерброды в дорогу" (sandwiches) or a generic lunch.

reason: Come alive was famously rendered in Chinese as "brings your ancestors back from the grave".
suggested_fix: Adapt the meaning, not the words, e.g. a youth/energy line like "新一代的选择".

reason: American football is niche in Russia, so the touchdown metaphor won't land.
suggested_fix: Use a neutral phrase, e.g. "Выгодная экономия с этими скидками."

reason: Pajero is vulgar slang in many Spanish-speaking markets (Mitsubishi famously sold it there as "Montero").
suggested_fix: Use an alternate market name for Spanish-speaking markets, such as "Montero".

reason: In Russia, constant smiling at strangers can read as insincere or odd. A "big smile" promise may not land as warmth.
suggested_fix: Emphasize attentive, friendly service instead, e.g. "Наши сотрудники всегда рады вам помочь."

reason: Nuts about (crazy about) plays on almonds being nuts. The wordplay is lost in Russian.
suggested_fix: Drop the pun, e.g. "Мы обожаем миндаль."

reason: Hey buddy is overly familiar for Russian customer messaging and forces an awkward ты-form.
suggested_fix: Use a neutral, polite form, e.g. "Ваш заказ доставлен!"

reason: Baseball is niche in Russia, so the home run metaphor won't land.
suggested_fix: Use a neutral phrase, e.g. "Сделайте свою следующую презентацию блестящей."

reason: Un-brie-lievable is cheese wordplay that can't be translated.
suggested_fix: Drop the pun, e.g. "Невероятные скидки на сыр."

reason: Thanksgiving is not celebrated in Russia.
suggested_fix: Tie the bundle to a local occasion, e.g. New Year, or present it as a family dinner set.

reason: Most Russians celebrate Orthodox Christmas on January 7. New Year is the main gift holiday, and December 25 is a regular workday.
suggested_fix: Reframe around New Year, e.g. "С Новым годом! Бесплатная доставка до 31 декабря."
